newsitem.title: UK: Overcapacity continues to depress insurance rates.
newsitem.headline: Overcapacity continues to depress insurance rates.

text.p: Increased competition and excess capacity continue to beset marine, aviation and energy insurance markets, according to the latest report from Britain's Institute of London Underwriters (ILU), released on Tuesday.

The ILU, which represents 53 of the largest companies operating in the London insurance market, said that while financial results had improved over the past three years, many underwriters were still finding it necessary to increase reserves for prior years.
The continuing tail of losses is reflected in this year's results with premiums amounting to 1,469 million stg and claims paid 2,085 million stg, the seventh successive year of negative cashflow.
ILU chairman Nigel Jenkins warned that continuing falls in rates would prove unsustainable.
"With the losses of recent years still fresh in our minds, it is hard to understand how we can be confonted with the scale of rate reductions we have seen in the hull and energy markets," he said.

While prices had sunk to "a very low ebb", particularly for hull and energy risks, the market had benefited from an absence of catastrophe losses, although the ILU said circumstances could quickly change.
"Catastrophes will inevitably occur. Premium rates must reflect the need to maintain adequate reserves," it said.

"The unavoidable erosion of profit margins may bring some collective sense back to the market, but really it is up to individual underwriters to stand firm and put underwriting profit before market share to achieve stability."
Premiums have fallen as excess capacity, reduced orders, self-insurance, falling rates and more recently the strength of the pound have taken their toll.

According to the ILU most classes of marine business had experienced a continuing drop in rates. Abundant capacity and increased competition could not excuse the "irresponsible underwriting that characterised much of the past year as some underwriters strove to maintain market share."
The downward pressure on rates was also evident in the energy market, fuelled as in hull insurance by fierce competition from within London and from overseas.
Despite the market conditions, Jenkins cautioned against concluding that the results would be indicative of any one company's results.

"I remain firmly convinced that those who prepare robust business plans, and carry them through, can still achieve a positive result," Jenkins said. "But those who are less rigorous will be unable to meet the expectations of capital providers in the current trading climate."

Although 1993 and 1994 underwriting and revenue figures showed a considerable improvement over the previous three years, the improvement levelled off in 1995 and 1996, the ILU said. It was too early to say if these years would produce a satisfactory result.
